objects.why: Darwin's Marry / Not Marry page, Franklin's moral algebra, the midnight legal pad - the two-column list the book calls an evaluation tool, not a discovery tool.
The recurring 'widen the map before you choose': two obvious roads and the invented third path (L'Enfant's park, the counter-offer, the two-year experiment).
The table-sized scale model of the Abbottabad compound the CIA studied for months.
The luxury houses built on filled-in Collect Pond that sank, flooded and became Five Points.
The dog in the compound - the contrary evidence the red team found.
The Black Hawk raid option whose lift in heat and altitude had to be modelled.
Tetlock's hedgehog: one big theory, one predicted future.
Tetlock's fox: many small ideas, multiple futures.
Weighing values: Franklin's cancelling, linear value modelling.
The premortem - the plan imagined already dead.
Messages to the stars; the far future.

spine.claim: Our worst decisions fail at the moment we accept only two options - Darwin's two-column list and the city that filled in Collect Pond instead of building L'Enfant's park.
A pros-and-cons list only evaluates; mapping hidden variables, a messy divergence phase and diverse rooms that surface hidden profiles discover the real terrain.
Predicting means telling several futures - Brennan's red team, scenario planning, foxes over hedgehogs, the 70% rule and the premortem that builds escape hatches.
Deciding means weighing values openly - Johnson's Brooklyn-or-California deadlock became an invented option C - and fiction like Middlemarch rehearses choices numbers cannot.
We rarely have nine months, so we train on the big choices until seeing wider is reflex: farsightedness is seeing wider, not further.

openingLines: So, we're dropping right into July of We're in this um rather cramped smoky room in London and the air is just thick with that early industrial soot.
You know, the kind that just completely coats the windows.
Oh, yeah. That gross gritty feeling.
Exactly. And sitting at a wooden desk is a 29-year-old Charles Darwin.
He has this blank leatherbound notebook open right in front of him.
He takes a pen, dips it in ink, and he rules a hard line straight down the middle of the page.
closingLines: We spend so much of our finite lives absolutely terrified of making the wrong choice.
We agonize over the columns on the legal pad.
But what if the greatest, most beautiful, most defining decisions you will ever make in your lifetime aren't about picking the right option at all?
What if they are the moments where you finally summon the courage to throw out option A and option B entirely, look at the terrifying blank space on the map, and invent option See?
